In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the left ventricular mechanics, both in the infarction-related and remote regions, after an ST-elevation acute myocardial infarct (STEMI) in patients with single vessel disease, who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention.
the development of new methods and techniques for the study of the mechanical behavior of the heart, and the application of these techniques in the study of patients with heart disease.
the study of left ventricular deformation and rotation in patients with single vessel disease after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarctions (STEMI) 2 years post revascularization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the present study, the presence of a single risk factor (e.g. hypertension), in addition to the presence of multiple factors, was related to the presence of left ventricular dilatation, independent of the infarction size.
the reduction in regional strains and torsion is a common finding in both the infact related and remote regions of a dilated left ventricular chamber.

, in patients with single vessel disease after an ST elevation myocardial infarct (STEMI), the global longitudinal strain (GLS), global circumferential strains (GCS) and global radial strain (GRS) are reduced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the left ventricular remodeling following an ST-ejection myocardial infarct is a multifactorial process, in which the reduction in regional strains, rather than the isolated changes in the infarction region might be the key factor in the determination of the left ventricular dilation.

we have shown that the changes in left ventricular mechanics in patients with a history of ST-elevation myocardical infarction (STEI-MI) and coronary revascularization are not limited to the infarct zone.

we have demonstrated that there are global changes in left ventricular function following an acute myocardial infarct, and these global changes are related to the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, despite the presence of multiple cardiovascular risk factors, the reduction in left ventricular strains in patients with single-vessel coronary artery disease 2 years after STEMI is not confined to the infarct zone, but is also present in the remote regions of the dilated left ventricles.

the reduction in regional strains and rotations in patients with single-vessel disease, 2 years after STEMI and percutaneous coronary intervention is not only limited to the infarcted myocardium but is also present in the remote noninfarcted myocardial segments.
the left ventricular remodeling is not limited to the infarct zone but it involves also the remote myocardium.
